newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: First vote on Boutros-Ghali candidacy on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: First vote on Boutros-Ghali candidacy on Tuesday.

text.p: The United States was isolated in opposing a second term for Boutros Boutros-Ghali as the Security Council met to pick a U.N. secretary-general, with a first vote expected on Tuesday.

In the first round of informal meetings, U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright told the 15-member council she was armed with instructions from Washington to block the re-election of Boutros-Ghali, whose term expires on December 31.

Her spokesman said the U.S. envoy warned members nations that the Republican-dominated Congress would not authorise payment of the more than $1 billion Washington owes the United Nations if Boutros-Ghali continued in the post.
Many on the council believe the Egyptian secretary-general has been made a scapegoat for failures in U.S. foreign policy and Republican opposition to the world body.
The United States, Britain, France, Russia and China all have veto power on the council.

A resolution drafted by Egypt, Guinea-Bissau and Botswana, the council's three African members, would support another term for Boutros-Ghali until the year 2001. It is expected to be put to a vote on Tuesday, Council president Nugroho Wisnumurti said.
Egypt's Ambassador Nabil Elaraby said he expected a vote of 14-1. "There will be 14 votes on record in favour. They (the members) told me," he said.
Other sources agreed with Elaraby's analysis. The resolution has 10 sponsors so far -- Russia, France, China, Egypt, Guinea-Bissau, Germany, Chile, Indonesia, Botswana and Honduras.

Not sponsoring the resolution, aside from the United States, are Britain, Poland, South Korea and Italy, indicating these nations may vote for another candidate once the stalemate over Boutros-Ghali is resolved.
British ambassador Sir John Weston told the council that while his country backed Boutros-Ghali, U.S. opposition had changed the picture and made it necessary to move on, diplomats said.

The purpose of the resolution is to put on record the council's overwhelming support for Boutros-Ghali and isolate the United States. Washington has been strongly criticised for using the New York Times to announce its opposition to Boutros-Ghali and for precipitating a financial crisis by refusing to pay the $1.4 billion it owes the United Nations.

If and when a veto is cast, council members would again consult and give preference to other African candidates on the grounds that if, contrary to U.N. practice, Boutros-Ghali was denied a second term, he should at least be succeeded by someone from his region of the world.

If the council is unable to choose an African, the contest would eventually be thrown open to candidates from other parts of the world, though it is unclear how many ballots might be confined exclusively to African hopefuls.

But in the confused procedures of the Security Council, France, a strong supporter of Boutros-Ghali that also has veto power, could block any other candidate, particularly one from a so-called "anglophone" country that the U.S. might favour.
Paris could argue that since 14 countries favoured Boutros-Ghali, the least the council could do was to support the 74-year old law professor for another two years.
U.S. sources said Indonesian President Suharto wrote a letter to President Bill Clinton saying Washington should consider such a compromise but the United States so far has rejected it.

Previously several world leaders were said to have written to Clinton, including Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, French President Jacques Chirac, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, South African President Nelson Mandela, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien and Honduran President Carlos Roberto Reina.

Among African diplomats mentioned as potential candidates are Under-Secretary-General Kofi Annan of Ghana, who heads U.N. peacekeeping operations; Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference; Salim A. Salim of Tanzania, the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity; Abdou Diouf, the president of Senegal; and Amara Essy, the foreign minister of the Ivory Coast.
